procedural_history.impugned_order: Order rejecting the bail application filed by the appellant (BLAPL No. 1855 of 2022). The High Court granted bail to the appellant on 11.10.2023, while the SLP was pending before the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a bail application (BLAPL No. 1855 of 2022) before the High Court. The High Court granted bail on 11.10.2023, but the order did not mention that it was the second bail application or the pendency of the SLP before the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) before the Supreme Court, aggrieved by the order rejecting his bail application. Notice was issued in the SLP in September 2023. The Supreme Court took note of the High Court granting bail without acknowledging the pending SLP and issued an order on 06.12.2023, requesting a report from the High Court. After receiving the report, the Supreme Court is now hearing Criminal Appeal No. 303 of 2024.

directions: We, therefore, quash and set aside the impugned order dated 31.01.2023 and remand the matter back to the High Court.
The High Court is requested to consider the effect of the orders passed by the other coordinate Benches and pass orders afresh.
The same shall be done within a period of one month from today.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is a mandatory prerequisite for an applicant to disclose the details of previously filed bail applications and their outcomes when filing a new application for bail.

facts: The case involved an appellant who, while a matter was pending before the Supreme Court, filed a second bail application before the High Court.
The appellant did not disclose the fact that a Special Leave Petition (SLP) related to the case was pending before the Supreme Court.
The appellant also failed to mention the rejection of the earlier bail application or the filing of the SLP in the list of dates provided to the High Court.
law: The Supreme Court established a mandatory rule to avoid confusion and streamline bail proceedings in the future.
application: The Court held that all applications for bail must mandatorily include specific details about prior applications.
Specifically, an applicant must provide: (1) Details and copies of orders from any earlier bail applications that have already been decided.

Additionally, the applicant must provide: (2) Details of any bail application that is currently pending in any court, whether higher or lower. If no application is pending, a clear statement to that effect must be made.

The Court also suggested other procedural measures, such as clearly labeling the application as 'first', 'second', etc., and having all bail applications from the same case listed before the same judge to avoid anomalies.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it is a mandatory prerequisite for an applicant to disclose the details of all previously filed bail applications, including their outcomes and any pending applications, when filing a new application for bail.

issue.issue_text: What is the effect of an applicant suppressing or concealing material facts, such as the filing and disposal of previous bail applications, when seeking bail from a court?

facts: The Court addressed the practice of applicants for bail not mentioning or concealing the details of their previous bail applications and the orders passed on them.

The Court noted that this practice of suppressing material facts leads to an "anomalous situation" where different outcomes (grant or refusal of bail) occur for co-accused individuals with similar roles in the same crime.
law: The act of suppressing material facts (suppressio veri) is detrimental to the administration of justice.
Counsels appearing for parties have a duty to act as "officers of the Court" and must not mislead the court through misrepresentation or suppression of facts.
application: To prevent these anomalies and streamline the process, the Court made it mandatory for all bail applications to include specific information.

The mandatory disclosures include: details and copies of orders from all previously decided bail applications, and details of any bail applications that are currently pending in any court (or a clear statement that none are pending).
The Court also suggested that applications should clearly state on top whether they are the "first, second or third and so on" to provide immediate context to the judge.

To support this, the Court directed that the court's Registry should annex a report on pending or decided bail applications for the case, and that the Investigating Officer has a duty to inform the State Counsel of any previous court orders.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that suppressing or concealing the history of previous bail applications is a serious issue that undermines the justice system. To rectify this, the Court made it a mandatory prerequisite for all bail applications to contain a full and clear disclosure of any prior or pending bail applications and their outcomes.

cases.case_name: K.D. Sharma Vs. Steel Authority of India Limited and others
cases.principle: An order obtained by practising fraud and suppressing a material fact before a court of law to gain an advantage cannot be allowed to stand.

cases.case_name: Pradhani Jani v. The State of Odisha
cases.principle: Advocates have a duty to diligently verify facts from the record of the case using their legal acumen and cannot be absolved of this responsibility by claiming they were merely acting on instructions from their clients.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order obtained by practicing fraud and suppressing material facts before a court of law cannot be allowed to stand. A litigant who attempts to pollute the stream of justice or who touches the pure fountain of justice with tainted hands by suppressing material facts is not entitled to any relief, interim or final. To avoid such situations in the future, it is mandatory to mention certain information in applications filed for grant of bail.
obiter: A very high standard of professionalism and legal acumen is expected from advocates, particularly designated Senior Advocates, and their duty to diligently verify facts from the record of the case cannot be obviated.

The materialism in the post-Independence era has overshadowed the old ethos of 'satya' (truth), leading to a rise in litigants who do not hesitate to take shelter of falsehood, misrepresentation, and suppression of facts in court proceedings.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An applicant seeking bail has a mandatory duty to make a full and correct disclosure of all material facts, including the details of previously filed bail applications and their outcomes. The suppression or concealment of such facts is not mere advocacy but a form of fraud on the court, an abuse of its process, and an act that pollutes the stream of justice. A litigant who approaches the court with 'soiled hands' by suppressing the truth is not entitled to any relief, and the court has the inherent power to protect itself by refusing to examine the case on its merits and may even hold the applicant in contempt.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that an applicant must approach the court with 'candid facts' and a 'clean breast', and cannot hold a writ of the court with 'soiled hands'. (Kensington Income Tax Commrs.)
The maxim 'supressio veri, expressio falsi', meaning the suppression of the truth is equivalent to the expression of falsehood.
The inherent power of the court to protect itself and prevent an abuse of its process when a party misleads it or suppresses material facts.
The principle that an order obtained by practicing fraud and suppressing material facts before a court of law cannot be allowed to stand.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant suppressed the material fact that a prior bail application had been rejected and that a challenge to that rejection was pending before the Supreme Court. This was a clear case of suppression of a fact within the appellant's special knowledge.
The court held that suppression or concealment of material facts is a jugglery, manipulation, or misrepresentation which has no place in equitable jurisdiction.
By not disclosing all material facts fairly and truly, the appellant misled the court, which is an abuse of the court's process.

The court equated the appellant's suppression of truth with the expression of falsehood, stating that such a litigant attempts to pollute the stream of justice and touches the pure fountain of justice with tainted hands, disentitling them to any relief.
The act of suppression was considered a fraud practiced upon the court to gain an advantage, rendering the order obtained unsustainable.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully demonstrated that the appellant had suppressed material facts by failing to disclose the rejection of the earlier bail application and the pendency of the Special Leave Petition before the Supreme Court.
The court accepted the respondent's position that this suppression was an attempt to pollute the stream of administration of justice and interfere with its proper course.
policy_considerations: The stream of administration of justice must remain unpolluted to maintain the sublimity of the court’s environment and give vitality to all organs of the State.

Litigants who take recourse to fraud or act with oblique motives interfere with the administration of justice and must be properly dealt with, not only for punishment but also to deter others from similar acts which shake public faith in the justice system.

The cherished basic value of 'satya' (truth) is an integral part of the justice-delivery system, and a litigant who takes shelter of falsehood, misrepresentation, and suppression of facts is not entitled to any relief.

The practice of filing successive bail applications without disclosing prior outcomes leads to anomalous situations where some accused are granted bail while others in similar circumstances are refused.

Advocates, as officers of the court, have a very high standard of professionalism and a duty to assist the court fairly, which includes diligently verifying facts from the record and not just acting on client instructions.
